tip: 受け取り方 (uketorikata, 'how you take/interpret something') extends this beyond physical objects — how you emotionally receive news or criticism.

sentence_jp: 荷物が届きました。
sentence_en: The package has arrived.
tip: 気持ちが届く (kimochi ga todoku, 'feelings reach someone') is a touching figurative use — emotions, like packages, can 'arrive' at their destination.

en: To be conveyed / To get across (a message)
sentence_jp: 気持ちが伝わってよかったです。
sentence_en: I'm glad my feelings got across.
tip: The intransitive partner of 伝える (tsutaeru, to convey) — this is what happens on the receiving end when a message successfully lands.

sentence_jp: 言葉で表すのが難しいです。
sentence_en: It's hard to express in words.
tip: 表情 (hyoujou, facial expression) shares this same character — both are about making an inner feeling visible on the outside.

sentence_jp: 税込みの価格には税金が含まれています。
sentence_en: The tax-included price has the tax included.
tip: 税込み (zeikomi, 'tax included') and 税抜き (zeinuki, 'tax excluded') are both everyday shopping terms built on related ideas of inclusion.

en: To be missing / To be chipped
sentence_jp: お皿が少し欠けています。
sentence_en: The plate is slightly chipped.
tip: 常識に欠ける (joushiki ni kakeru, 'lacking common sense') extends this verb into criticizing someone's judgment or manners.

en: To make up for / To supplement
sentence_jp: 経験不足を努力で補いました。
sentence_en: I made up for my lack of experience with effort.
tip: 栄養を補う (eiyou wo oginau, 'to supplement nutrition') is a common phrase in health and supplement advertising.

sentence_jp: 優れた技術力を持っています。
sentence_en: They have excellent technical skill.
tip: 優れた (sugureta, the past-tense adjectival form) is used constantly in product descriptions — '優れた品質' means 'superior quality.'

sentence_jp: 性能は他社製品に劣りません。
sentence_en: The performance is not inferior to other companies' products.
tip: Often used in the negative, as here — 劣らない (otoranai, 'not inferior to') is a common, humble way to claim something is just as good, without boasting outright.

en: To be complete / To be all gathered
sentence_jp: メンバーが全員揃いました。
sentence_en: All the members are gathered.
tip: お揃い (osoroi) means 'matching' (as in matching outfits) — a beloved concept for Japanese friend groups and couples.

sentence_jp: お金が足りません。
sentence_en: I don't have enough money.
tip: 物足りない (monotarinai, literally 'thing-not-enough') means 'unsatisfying' or 'lacking something' — a very natural, useful compound.

en: To be left over / To be in excess
sentence_jp: 料理が少し余りました。
sentence_en: A little bit of the food was left over.
tip: 手に余る (te ni amaru, 'too much for one's hands') idiomatically means a task is beyond your ability to handle.

sentence_jp: 予定が重なってしまいました。
sentence_en: My plans ended up overlapping.
tip: Used for schedules clashing, but also literally for physical objects stacking or overlapping — 重なる本 (books stacked on each other).

sentence_jp: 電車が大きく揺れました。
sentence_en: The train shook violently.
tip: Essential earthquake vocabulary — 地震で揺れる (jishin de yureru, 'shaking from an earthquake') is a phrase every resident of Japan learns quickly.

sentence_jp: 夕日が海に沈みます。
sentence_en: The sunset sinks into the sea.
tip: 気分が沈む (kibun ga shizumu, 'one's mood sinks') figuratively extends this to describe feeling down or depressed.

en: To float / To come to mind
sentence_jp: いいアイデアが浮かびました。
sentence_en: A good idea came to mind.
tip: Used both literally (an object floating) and mentally (an idea 'floating up' into your consciousness) — a lovely shared image.

sentence_jp: その言葉が心に響きました。
sentence_en: Those words resonated deeply with me.
tip: 心に響く (kokoro ni hibiku, 'to resonate in the heart') is a beautiful, common phrase for describing something emotionally moving.

en: To soak in / To sting (of pain)
sentence_jp: 傷口に染みました。
sentence_en: It stung on the wound.
tip: Also used figuratively for something soaking into your understanding or emotions over time — 身に染みる (mi ni shimiru), 'to really hit home.'

sentence_jp: 記憶が少しずつ薄れています。
sentence_en: The memory is gradually fading.
tip: 薄い (usui, 'thin/faint') is the adjective root — this verb describes something gradually thinning out until it's nearly gone.

sentence_jp: 秋が深まってきました。
sentence_en: Autumn has been deepening.
tip: 秋が深まる (aki ga fukamaru, 'autumn deepens') is a poetic, seasonally beloved phrase describing the progression toward late autumn.

en: To be soothed / To feel at ease
sentence_jp: 猫を見ると心が和みます。
sentence_en: Seeing cats soothes my heart.
tip: 和 (wa, harmony) is the same character central to 'Japan' itself (和食, 和室, etc.) — this verb is that harmony settling gently into your mood.

en: To be healed / To feel soothed
sentence_jp: 自然の中で癒されました。
sentence_en: I felt healed and at peace out in nature.
tip: 癒し (iyashi, 'healing/comfort') became a huge cultural buzzword in the 1990s and remains central to how wellness is marketed in Japan today.

en: To fit in / To become familiar
sentence_jp: 新しい職場にだいぶ馴染みました。
sentence_en: I've settled in quite well at the new workplace.
tip: 馴染みの店 (najimi no mise, 'a regular/familiar shop') describes a favorite spot you visit so often the staff know you.

en: To open up / To warm up to someone
sentence_jp: すぐにみんなと打ち解けました。
sentence_en: I quickly opened up to everyone.
tip: 打つ (to strike) + 解ける (to melt/dissolve) — the image of a barrier between people literally melting away through friendly contact.

sentence_jp: 友達を励ましました。
sentence_en: I encouraged my friend.
tip: 励まし (hagemashi, noun form) means 'encouragement.' 励まし合う (hagemashiau) — 'to encourage each other' — describes mutual support.

sentence_jp: 髪を触るのが癖です。
sentence_en: Touching my hair is a habit of mine.
tip: Distinct from 習慣 (a deliberate, positive habit) — 癖 often refers to a small, unconscious quirk, sometimes slightly negative.

sentence_jp: 個性を大切にしましょう。
sentence_en: Let's value individuality.
tip: 個性的 (koseiteki, 'individualistic/unique') is a genuine compliment in modern Japan, even as conformity is often stereotyped as the cultural norm.

sentence_jp: あなたの長所は何ですか。
sentence_en: What are your strong points?
tip: A near-mandatory job interview question in Japan — 長所と短所 (chousho to tansho, 'strengths and weaknesses') is the classic pairing.

sentence_jp: 短所は心配性なところです。
sentence_en: My weak point is that I tend to worry a lot.
tip: The natural partner to 長所 above — a common self-reflection pair used constantly in résumés and interviews.

sentence_jp: 彼女は向上心が強いです。
sentence_en: She has a strong drive to improve herself.
tip: 向上 (improvement/rising) + 心 (heart/spirit) — a prized trait in Japanese resumes and self-descriptions, valuing growth over static achievement.

en: Inquisitive spirit / Curiosity to explore deeply
sentence_jp: 子供の探究心を伸ばしたいです。
sentence_en: I want to nurture children's inquisitive spirits.
tip: 探究 (deep inquiry) + 心 (spirit) — often used in education contexts, describing a drive to dig deeper rather than accept surface answers.

sentence_jp: 彼女はおおらかな性格です。
sentence_en: She has an easygoing, big-hearted personality.
tip: Praises someone who doesn't sweat small stuff — unbothered by details in a warm, generous way rather than a careless one.

sentence_jp: 彼は繊細な心の持ち主です。
sentence_en: He has a sensitive, delicate heart.
tip: Used for both emotional sensitivity and physical delicacy — 繊細な作業 (sensai na sagyou) means 'delicate, precise work,' like fine craftsmanship.

sentence_jp: 大胆な決断をしました。
sentence_en: I made a bold decision.
tip: 大胆不敵 (daitan futeki) is a fuller four-character phrase meaning 'boldly fearless' — describing someone unshakeable in the face of risk.

sentence_jp: 慎重に運転してください。
sentence_en: Please drive carefully / cautiously.
tip: The natural opposite of 大胆 above — 慎重派 (shinchouha) describes someone who is by nature a careful, deliberate planner.

sentence_jp: 柔軟な考え方が大切です。
sentence_en: A flexible way of thinking is important.
tip: Used for physical flexibility (柔軟体操, stretching exercises) and mental flexibility (柔軟な発想, flexible thinking) alike.

sentence_jp: 祖父はとても頑固です。
sentence_en: My grandfather is very stubborn.
tip: 頑固親父 (ganko oyaji, 'stubborn old man') is a beloved cultural archetype — the gruff, set-in-his-ways craftsman or shopkeeper.

sentence_jp: 派手な服が好きです。
sentence_en: I like flashy clothes.
tip: Its opposite, 地味 (jimi, plain/subdued), is used just as often — Japanese fashion vocabulary frequently contrasts these two.

sentence_jp: 今日は地味な格好をしています。
sentence_en: I'm dressed plainly / low-key today.
tip: Not necessarily negative — 地味だけど大切な仕事 (jimi dakedo taisetsu na shigoto) means 'unglamorous but important work,' a common respectful phrase.

en: A good problem to have (a luxurious worry)
sentence_jp: それは贅沢な悩みですね。
sentence_en: Well, that's a good problem to have.
tip: Used lightly, often with a touch of gentle envy — like having to choose between three great job offers.

en: It's darkest under the lighthouse (blind to what's close)
sentence_jp: 灯台下暗しで、探していた鍵は目の前にありました。
sentence_en: Talk about not seeing what's right in front of you — the key I was looking for was right there.
tip: You'd expect a lighthouse to illuminate everything, but its own base sits in shadow — a poetic warning about overlooking the obvious.

en: An iron club for an ogre (making the strong even stronger)
sentence_jp: 経験に加えて資格も取れば鬼に金棒です。
sentence_en: If you add a qualification on top of your experience, it'll make you unstoppable.
tip: An oni (demon/ogre) is already fearsome — give it an iron club too, and nothing can stand in its way. Used for a winning combination.

reading: こうぼうにもふでのあやまり
romaji: koubou ni mo fude no ayamari
en: Even the great calligrapher Kobo makes a slip of the brush
sentence_jp: 弘法にも筆の誤りで、私も間違えることがあります。
sentence_en: Even the best make mistakes sometimes — I make errors too.
tip: Named for Kukai (Kobo Daishi), a legendary Japanese calligrapher — even a master's hand slips occasionally. The Japanese 'even Homer nods.'

en: Writhing in agony (falling seven times, rolling eight)
sentence_jp: 歯痛で七転八倒しました。
sentence_en: I was writhing in agony from a toothache.
tip: Visually related to 七転び八起き (fall seven, rise eight) but describes acute physical or mental suffering rather than resilience.

en: Rapid, constant progress (daily advance, monthly step)
sentence_jp: テクノロジーは日進月歩で発展しています。
sentence_en: Technology is developing with rapid, constant progress.
tip: Often used for describing fast-moving fields like technology or medicine — progress happening almost too fast to track.

en: To mutually improve through friendly rivalry
sentence_jp: ライバルと切磋琢磨しています。
sentence_en: My rival and I push each other to improve.
tip: Originally describes the polishing of gemstones — the idea that friction between two ambitious people sharpens both, like stones polishing each other.

en: A dramatic comeback (bringing the dying back to life)
sentence_jp: 起死回生のホームランでした。
sentence_en: It was a dramatic, game-saving home run.
tip: Literally 'raising the dead, returning to life' — used for last-minute reversals in sports, business, or any nearly-lost situation turned around.
